title: Around Town
summary: Say where things are, where you come from and where you go: the six location cases with consonant gradation, in town and on the move.

lessons.title: Places in town
lessons.objective: Name everyday places in town and ask where something is.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: English uses small words like *in*, *from* and *to*. Finnish adds an ending to the noun instead: `koulu|ssa` = in the school. There are six such endings, the **location cases**. Each one answers a question: `Missä?` (where?), `Mistä?` (from where?) or `Mihin?` (to where?). First, learn the places themselves.

items.en: Excuse me, where is the post office?
The post office is over there.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: All three questions start with `mi-`. Listen to the end: `Missä?` sits still (where at?), `Mistä?` moves away (from where?), `Mihin?` moves in (to where?). You will also hear `Minne?`: it means the same as `Mihin?`.

cards.title: Watch out
cards.body: Finnish has no *a* or *the*. `kauppa` is *a shop* or *the shop*. Don't look for an article: just say `Kauppa on tuolla.`

cards.title: Good to know
cards.body: A `terveyskeskus` is the public health centre, where you see a doctor or a nurse. An `apteekki` is where you buy medicine. Both words come up often in tasks about everyday life in Finland.

terms.say: Six noun endings that say where something is, where it comes from and where it goes. They do the job of English in, at, from and to.

lessons.title: In: -ssa / -ssä
lessons.objective: Say where someone or something is with the inessive.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: The **inessive** means *in* or *inside*. Add **-ssa** or **-ssä** to the word: `koulu` → `koulu|ssa` (in the school). It answers `Missä?` (where?). Use it with `olla` (to be) and `asua` (to live): `Olen koulussa.` `Asun Oulussa.`

cards.title: -ssa or -ssä?
cards.body: This is **vowel harmony** from World 1. If the word has a, o or u, use **-ssa**: `talossa`, `kirjastossa`. If it has none of them (only ä, ö, y, e, i), use **-ssä**: `kylässä`, `Jyväskylässä`. `posti` has an o, so `postissa`.

items.en: Are you at the post office?

cards.title: Watch out
cards.body: The ending goes straight onto the word. Don't change the last vowel: `koulu` → `koulussa`, not *koulossa*. Write the double s: `talossa`, not *talosa*.

cards.title: Same question, same ending
cards.body: The question and the answer match: `Missä asut?` – `Asun Kuopiossa.` `Missä olet?` – `Olen kirjastossa.` Answer with the place + -ssa / -ssä.

terms.say: The 'in' case. Ending -ssa or -ssä. It answers Missä? (where?): talossa = in the house.
A Finnish word uses either back vowels (a, o, u) or front vowels (ä, ö, y) in its endings, never both. e and i fit with either.

lessons.title: Gradation: kk, pp, tt
lessons.objective: Make the weak grade of kk, pp and tt words before an ending.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Many Finnish words change a consonant when you add an ending. This is **consonant gradation**. The basic form has the **strong grade**: `kauppa`. With -ssa the syllable closes and the consonant gets the **weak grade**: `kaupa|ssa`. A double consonant becomes single: **kk → k, pp → p, tt → t**.

cards.title: One weak stem, many endings
cards.body: These endings all take the weak grade: **-ssa, -sta, -lla, -lta, -lle**. Learn the weak stem once (`kaupa-`) and reuse it: `kaupassa`, `kaupasta`. One ending is different, the *to* form; it comes in a later lesson.

cards.title: Watch out
cards.body: Only the consonant before the last vowel changes. `kauppakeskus` (shopping centre) keeps its pp: `kauppakeskuksessa`. Words without kk, pp or tt there don't change: `posti` → `postissa`, `koulu` → `koulussa`.

terms.say: A change of k, p or t inside a word when an ending is added: kauppa → kaupassa. Finnish speakers do it without thinking.
The consonant as it is in the basic form, for example pp in kauppa.
The shorter or softer consonant before most endings, for example p in kaupassa.

lessons.title: More gradation
lessons.objective: Recognise the other strong → weak patterns in place names and common words.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Gradation also changes single consonants and pairs. **k → ∅** (the k disappears): `Turku` → `Turussa`. **p → v**: `leipä` → `leivässä`. **t → d**: `katu` → `kadulla`. The weak form is the **stem** you add the ending to: `Turu-`, `leivä-`, `kadu-`.

items.en: Do you live in the city?
The car is on the street.

cards.title: Some -i words change to e
cards.body: Many old -i words have an **e** stem: `Suomi` → `Suomessa`, `joki` (river) → `joessa`, `Lahti` → `Lahdessa`, `lampi` → `lammessa`. Newer words keep the i: `posti` → `postissa`, `bussi` → `bussissa`, `pankki` → `pankissa`. The second form on a flashcard (`Suomen`, `postin`) shows you the stem.

cards.title: Learn the pairs
cards.body: Say the pairs aloud as one chunk: `Helsinki – Helsingissä`, `Turku – Turussa`, `katu – kadulla`. You meet these words every day, so they stick fast.

terms.say: The part of the word that the ending is added to. It can differ from the basic form: the stem of katu is kadu- in kadulla.

lessons.title: Out of: -sta / -stä
lessons.objective: Say where you come from with the elative.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: The **elative** means *out of* or *from inside*. The ending is **-sta / -stä**. It answers `Mistä?` (from where?). It uses the same weak stem as -ssa: `kaupa|ssa` → `kaupa|sta`, `Turu|ssa` → `Turu|sta`. You already know it from World 1: `Olen kotoisin Englannista.`

items.en: She is coming from the shop.

cards.title: One letter apart
cards.body: -ssa and -sta differ by one letter, so listen closely: `kaupassa` (in the shop), `kaupasta` (from the shop). Think of the **t** as a *takeoff*: you leave the place.

cards.title: Watch out
cards.body: Verbs of coming and leaving use -sta, not -ssa: `Tulen kaupasta.`, not *Tulen kaupassa*. Ask yourself: am I still there, or moving away from it?

terms.say: The 'out of' case. Ending -sta or -stä. It answers Mistä? (from where?): talosta = out of the house.

lessons.title: Into: the illative
lessons.objective: Say where you are going with the illative, keeping the strong grade.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: The **illative** means *into* or *to*. It answers `Mihin?` (to where?). Main rule: repeat the last vowel and add **-n**: `talo` → `taloon`, `koulu` → `kouluun`, `kauppa` → `kauppaan`, `posti` → `postiin`. Use it with `mennä` (to go): `Menen kouluun.`

cards.title: Two more patterns
cards.body: **One syllable with a long vowel or a vowel pair**: h + that vowel + n: `maa` → `maahan`, `työ` → `työhön`, `tie` (road) → `tiehen`. **A long vowel at the end of a longer stem**: **-seen**: `Espoo` → `Espooseen`, `Vantaa` → `Vantaaseen`, `huone` (room, stem `huonee-`) → `huoneeseen`.

cards.title: The illative stays strong
cards.body: Unlike -ssa, the illative keeps the **strong grade**: `kauppa` → `kauppaan` (not *kaupaan*), `pankki` → `pankkiin`, `Turku` → `Turkuun`, `Helsinki` → `Helsinkiin`. The syllable stays open: *kaup-pa-an*.

items.en: He is going to the bank.

cards.title: Watch out
cards.body: Start from the stem, not the basic form. `Suomi` has the stem `Suome-`, so `Suomeen`. Words in -us have the stem `-ukse-`: `terveyskeskus` → `terveyskeskukseen`. And double the vowel: `kouluun`, not *koulun* (that means *the school's*).

terms.say: The 'into' case. It answers Mihin? (to where?). Usually the last vowel doubles + n: taloon = into the house. It keeps the strong grade: kauppaan.

lessons.title: On, at, by: -lla / -llä
lessons.objective: Say where you are at open places and how you travel, with the adessive.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: The **adessive** means *on* or *at*. The ending is **-lla / -llä**: `asema` → `asema|lla` (at the station), `tori` → `tori|lla` (at the market square), `pöytä` → `pöydä|llä` (on the table). It also answers `Missä?`. Use it for open places and surfaces, not for being inside a building.

cards.title: By bus, by train
cards.body: The adessive also says **how you travel**. It answers `Millä?` (by what?): `bussilla` (by bus), `junalla` (by train), `autolla` (by car), `pyörällä` (by bike), `metrolla`, `taksilla`. On foot is `kävellen`. `Menen kouluun bussilla.` = I go to school by bus.

items.en: The bus is at the stop.
The car is on the street.
I go to school by bike.

cards.title: In the bus or by bus?
cards.body: `bussilla` = by bus (how you travel). `bussissa` = in the bus (where you sit now). Text a friend `Olen bussissa.` when you are on it. The same goes for `junassa` (on the train) and `junalla` (by train).

cards.title: Same weak stem
cards.body: Gradation works just like with -ssa: `pysäkki` → `pysäkillä`, `katu` → `kadulla`, `lentokenttä` → `lentokentällä`. One weak stem, many endings.

terms.say: The 'on / at' case. Ending -lla or -llä. Used for open places (asemalla), surfaces (pöydällä) and ways of travel (bussilla).

lessons.title: From and to: -lta / -lle
lessons.objective: Say where you come from and go to at open places, with the ablative and allative.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Open places have their own *from* and *to*. The **ablative** -lta / -ltä means *from* (off, away from): `asemalta` (from the station). The **allative** -lle means *to* (onto): `asemalle` (to the station). Both use the weak stem: `pysäkiltä`, `pysäkille`.

items.en: The train leaves from the station.
I'm going to the market square.
I'm coming from the airport by taxi.
The bus goes to the airport.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: -lle has only one form: it is always **-lle** (`torille`, `pysäkille`). -lta has two, by vowel harmony: `torilta`, but `pysäkiltä`.

cards.title: Watch out
cards.body: Keep a place in its own set. If it takes -lla, it also takes -lta and -lle: `asemalla – asemalta – asemalle`. `asemaan` would mean *into the station building*, which is not what you usually want.

terms.say: The 'from (off)' case for open places. Ending -lta or -ltä: asemalta = from the station.
The 'to (onto)' case for open places. Ending -lle: asemalle = to the station.

lessons.title: Inner or outer?
lessons.objective: Choose the inner or outer cases for places, cities, home and work.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: The six cases come in two sets. The **inner cases** (-ssa, -sta, the illative) are for inside: buildings, rooms, most towns and countries. The **outer cases** (-lla, -lta, -lle) are for open places and surfaces: station, market square, street, stop, airport. Learn each place with its set.

cards.title: Towns and cities
cards.body: Most towns take the inner cases: `Helsingissä`, `Turussa`, `Oulussa`, `Espoossa`. A few take the outer cases: `Tampereella`, `Vantaalla`, `Rovaniemellä`. There is no simple rule, so learn your own town with its three forms.

cards.title: Home and work
head: Basic form
Missä?
Mistä?
Mihin?
cards.body: Special forms: learn them as fixed chunks.

items.en: I come from work at five.

cards.title: Watch out
cards.body: At home is `kotona`, not *kodissa* (that means inside a home building). In everyday Finnish, work is `töissä`, `töistä`, `töihin`. The forms `työssä`, `työstä` and `työhön` are also correct, but sound more formal.

cards.title: In town or around town?
cards.body: `kaupungissa` = in the city (where you live). `kaupungilla` = out and about in town, for example shopping or walking. Both are correct, with different meanings.

terms.say: -ssa, -sta and the illative (-Vn). For being in, coming out of and going into a place.
-lla, -lta and -lle. For being at, coming from and going to an open place or a surface.

lessons.title: Go, come, be
lessons.objective: Pair mennä, tulla and olla with the right location case.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Each verb asks its own question. `olla` and `asua` (be, live) ask `Missä?`: -ssa / -lla. `tulla` (come) usually asks `Mistä?`: -sta / -lta. `mennä` (go) asks `Mihin?`: the illative / -lle. `tulla` can also take `Mihin?` when you come *to* a place: `Tulen kotiin.` = I'm coming home.

cards.title: mennä and tulla
head: mennä (go)
tulla (come)
cards.body: These are verb type 3, coming in World 3. For now, learn the forms by heart.

items.en: We are coming from Tampere by train.
I'm not going to work today.

cards.title: Ask the verb's question
cards.body: Before you add an ending, ask the verb's question. *Menen…* → Mihin? → `kauppaan`. *Olen…* → Missä? → `kaupassa`. *Tulen…* → Mistä? → `kaupasta`. Three questions, three forms of one word.

cards.title: Watch out
cards.body: English often says *at* for both being and going (*I'm at the shop*, *I'll go to the shop*). Finnish is strict: movement needs a *to* case. *Menen kaupassa* is wrong; say `Menen kauppaan.`

lessons.title: Asking the way
lessons.objective: Ask for and give simple directions in town.

items.en: Excuse me, where is the station?
The station is on the right.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Directions use the cases you know. `oikealla` / `vasemmalla` (-lla) = **on** the right / left: where something is. `oikealle` / `vasemmalle` (-lle) = **to** the right / left: where you turn. `suoraan` = straight ahead, `lähellä` = near, `kaukana` = far.

cards.title: Small words for a route
cards.body: `ensin` = first, `sitten` = then, `ja` = and. They make a clear route: `Ensin menet suoraan, sitten käännyt oikealle.`

cards.title: Watch out
cards.body: `kääntyä` (to turn) has gradation too: nt → nn. `minä käännyn`, `sinä käännyt`, but `hän kääntyy`. And `vasen` has the stem `vasemma-`: `vasemmalla`, `vasemmalle`.

cards.title: You'll hear orders
cards.body: People often give directions in the **imperative**: `Mene suoraan!` `Käänny vasemmalle!` It comes in a later world. When you give directions yourself, the present tense works well: `Menet suoraan. Käännyt vasemmalle.`

terms.say: The verb form for orders and instructions: Mene! = Go! Käänny! = Turn!

lessons.title: Meeting messages
lessons.objective: Write and understand short messages about where and when to meet.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: A meeting message needs three things: **where**, **when** and **how**. `Nähdään asemalla kello kuusi.` = See you at the station at six. `Nähdään` is a fixed **chunk**: learn it whole. Then add the place in its *where* form.

items.en: See you in the café at three.
See you at the market square tomorrow.
I'll wait for you at the station.

cards.title: myöhässä
cards.body: `myöhässä` (late) looks like an -ssä form, and it is one. Use it with `olla`: `Bussi on myöhässä.` `Olen myöhässä.` = I'm late.

cards.title: Open and close
cards.body: Start and end every message: `Hei Mari!` … `Terveisin, Sami`, or `Moi!` … and your name. YKI writing tasks ask you to remember the opening and the closing.

cards.title: In speech
cards.body: In speech you'll hear `mä oon asemalla` for `minä olen asemalla`. In writing, use the standard form.

terms.say: A group of words you learn as one piece, without taking it apart: Nähdään! = See you!

questions.explain: apteekki = pharmacy: the place where you buy medicine.

wrong: Missä? = where (at)? It asks where something is.
questions.explain: Mihin? asks where something goes. Missä? (where at) and Mistä? (from where) are the other two place questions.

questions.audio: Anteeksi, missä on terveyskeskus? – Terveyskeskus on tuolla. Se on lähellä.
questions.q: What is the person looking for?
questions.explain: terveyskeskus = health centre. The answer says it is over there (tuolla) and near (lähellä).
Missä? asks where something is. Missä on posti? = Where is the post office?

questions.q: Build the question: “Where is the library?”
questions.explain: Question word first, then the verb on, then the place: Missä on kirjasto?
Inessive -ssa = in. koulu has o and u (back vowels), so the ending is -ssa: koulu|ssa.
Vowel harmony: Jyväskylä has no a, o or u, so the ending is -ssä: Jyväskylä|ssä.
posti has o (a back vowel), so the inessive is -ssa: posti|ssa. The i words with o, a or u still take -ssa.

questions.q: Which form is right? *Asun pienessä ___.* (kylä = village)
wrong: Mixed harmony: kylä has ä and y, so the ending must be -ssä too.
Don't change the ä of the word: kylä stays kylä-.
kylä is the basic form; 'in' needs the ending -ssä.
questions.explain: kylä has only front vowels (y, ä), so the inessive is -ssä: kylä|ssä.

questions.q: Build the sentence: “I live in Oulu.”
questions.explain: Subject, verb, place: Minä asun Oulussa. Oulu + -ssa (back vowels o, u).

questions.audio: Hei, olen Mika. Asun Kuopiossa. Nyt olen kirjastossa.
questions.explain: Nyt olen kirjastossa = Now I am in the library. Kuopiossa is the town where he lives.
Gradation pp → p: kauppa → kaupa|ssa. The -ssa ending takes the weak grade.
Gradation kk → k: pankki → panki|ssa. Only one k before -ssa.
Gradation kk → k: apteekki → apteeki|ssa. The long ee doesn't change, only the kk.
Gradation tt → t: konsertti → konserti|ssa. Inessive -ssa because of the o.

wrong: No gradation: before -ssa, kk must become k.
The ending is -ssa with a double s.
questions.explain: kk → k before -ssa: kirkko → kirko|ssa.

questions.q: Which word does **not** change its consonants before -ssa?
questions.explain: posti has st, which is not a gradation pair, so it stays: postissa. kk, pp and tt all become single.

questions.q: Build the question: “Is Liisa in the bank?”
questions.explain: Yes/no questions put the verb with -ko first (World 1): Onko…? Then the person, then the place: pankki → pankissa (kk → k).
Gradation k → ∅: the k disappears. Turku → Turu|ssa.
Gradation nk → ng: Helsinki → Helsingi|ssä. The word has only i and e, so the ending is -ssä.
Gradation nt → nn: Lappeenranta → Lappeenranna|ssa. Back vowels a, so -ssa.
Suomi has an e stem: Suome-. Add -ssa (it has u and o): Suome|ssa.

questions.q: What is the weak stem of *katu* (street)?
wrong: That is the strong grade; endings like -lla need the weak one.
Gradation makes it weaker, never stronger.
questions.explain: Gradation t → d: katu → kadu-, as in kadulla (on the street).
In Helsinki the nk becomes ng in the weak grade: Helsingissä.

questions.audio: Moi! Olen Sara. Olen kotoisin Turusta, mutta asun nyt Helsingissä.
wrong: Turusta = from Turku: that is where she is from.
questions.explain: asun nyt Helsingissä = I live in Helsinki now (nk → ng + -ssä).

questions.q: Build the question: “Do you live in Helsinki?”
questions.explain: Verb + -ko first, then the subject, then the place: Asutko sinä Helsingissä? (nk → ng).
Elative -sta = out of, from inside. koulu has back vowels: koulu|sta.
Elative -sta uses the weak grade like -ssa: kauppa → kaupa|sta (pp → p).
kotoisin + elative. Turku → Turu|sta (k → ∅).

questions.q: Which sentence means *I am coming out of the bank*?
wrong: Olen pankissa = I am in the bank.
Menen pankkiin = I am going into the bank.
questions.explain: tulla + elative: pankki → panki|sta (kk → k).

questions.audio: Hei Pekka! Missä sinä olet? – Hei! Tulen nyt apteekista.
questions.explain: apteekista = from the pharmacy: apteekki → apteeki|sta (kk → k).

questions.q: Build the question: “Where are you coming from?”
questions.explain: Mistä? (from where?) goes with tulla. Question word, subject, verb: Mistä sinä tulet?
Illative: repeat the last vowel and add -n: koulu → koulu|un.
The illative keeps the strong grade: kauppa → kauppa|an (not kaupaan).
muuttaa (to move house) + illative. Strong grade nk stays: Helsinki → Helsinki|in.
Words in -us have the stem -ukse-: terveyskeskukse-. Repeat the e and add -n: terveyskeskukse|en.
Suomi has the stem Suome-. Repeat the e and add -n: Suome|en.

questions.q: Which is the illative (*to where?*) of *maa* (country)?
wrong: Three vowels in a row are not possible; one-syllable words with a long vowel take h + vowel + n.
-seen is for longer words like Espoo → Espooseen.
questions.explain: One syllable with a long vowel: h + the vowel + n: maa → maa|han.

questions.q: Which sentence means *I'm going into the shop*?
wrong: Olen kaupassa = I'm in the shop.
Tulen kaupasta = I'm coming from the shop.
The illative keeps the strong grade pp: kauppaan.
questions.explain: mennä + illative = going into: kauppa → kauppaan (strong grade kept).

questions.audio: Hei! Menen nyt kauppaan. Sitten menen postiin. Tuletko sinä kirjastoon?
questions.q: Where is the speaker going first?
wrong: The post office is second (sitten = then).
The speaker asks if YOU are coming to the library.
questions.explain: Menen nyt kauppaan = I'm going to the shop now. Sitten (then) postiin.

questions.q: Build the sentence: “We are going to Turku.”
questions.explain: mennä + illative. Turku keeps the strong grade rk in the illative: Turku|un.
Adessive -lla = on, at. A station is an outer place: asema|lla.
Adessive with kk → k: pysäkki → pysäki|llä. Front vowels y, ä, so -llä.
The adessive says how you travel (Millä? by what?): juna|lla.
Adessive with t → d: katu → kadu|lla.

questions.q: Your friend asks where you are. You're sitting in the bus. What do you write?
wrong: bussilla = by bus: how you travel, not where you are sitting.
questions.explain: Inside a vehicle = inessive -ssa: Olen bussissa. bussilla = by bus.

questions.audio: Hei, olen nyt asemalla. Juna on myöhässä. Tulen bussilla.
wrong: The train is late (juna on myöhässä), so the speaker takes the bus.
questions.explain: Tulen bussilla = I'll come by bus. The adessive -lla says how you travel.

questions.q: Build the question: “Is the bus at the stop?”
questions.explain: Onko first (-ko question), then the subject, then the place: pysäkki → pysäkillä (kk → k).
Ablative -lta = from (an outer place). asema|lta.
Allative -lle = to (an outer place). tori|lle. -lle is the same for all words.
Ablative with tt → t and front vowels: lentokentä|ltä.
Allative with tt → t: lentokentä|lle.

questions.q: Which is the ablative (*from*, outer case) of *katu*?
questions.explain: Ablative -lta with t → d: kadu|lta.

questions.q: *Tuletko ___?* = Are you coming from the market square? Which form fits?
wrong: tori is an outer place, so it takes -lta, not -sta.
questions.explain: tori takes the outer cases: torilla – torilta – torille. From = -lta.

questions.audio: Juna Tampereelle lähtee raiteelta kolme kello kaksi.
wrong: Tampereelle (-lle) = to Tampere; from would be Tampereelta.
raiteelta kolme = from track three: the train leaves from there.
questions.explain: Tampereelle = to Tampere (allative). raiteelta = from the track (ablative).

questions.q: Build the question: “Is the bus coming from the airport?”
questions.explain: tulla + ablative for an outer place: lentokenttä → lentokentältä (tt → t).
Tampere is one of the cities that take the outer cases: Tampere|ella (stem Tamperee-).
At work = töissä (everyday form). työssä is also correct, a little more formal.
koti → kotiin = (to) home. Repeat the i and add -n; the illative keeps the strong grade t.
At home is the special form kotona, not kodissa.
From work = töistä (everyday form); työstä is also correct.
Most cities take -ssa, but a few take -lla: Tampereella, Vantaalla, Rovaniemellä.
questions.source: Uusi kielemme: Places in Finnish (inner and outer cases)

questions.q: Kalle is at home. Which sentence says it?
wrong: kodissa = inside a home building; at home is kotona.
Not a word: no gradation and the wrong form.
questions.explain: olla + kotona = to be at home. koti has special forms: kotona, kotoa, kotiin.

questions.audio: Hei! Olen vielä töissä. Tulen kotiin kello kuusi. Menen ensin kauppaan.
wrong: kotiin = (to) home: the speaker goes there later.
kauppaan = to the shop: that comes next.
questions.explain: Olen vielä töissä = I'm still at work.
questions.source: Uusi kielemme: Places in Finnish (inner and outer cases)

questions.q: Build the sentence: “I'm going to work by bus.”
questions.explain: mennä + töihin (to work) + bussilla (by bus). Both orders are fine.
mennä: me menemme. Going into the shop, so the illative kauppaan.
tulla: he tulevat. Coming from = elative Oulusta.
olla: sinä olet + -ko → Oletko? Being at home = kotona.
Negation (World 1): en + the verb stem. mennä → mene: En mene töihin.

wrong: menee = goes; going needs the illative: kirjastoon.
tulee = comes; coming needs -sta (kirjastosta) or the illative.
menen = I go, and going needs kirjastoon.
questions.explain: kirjastossa answers Missä? (being somewhere), so the verb is olla: Hän on kirjastossa.

wrong: kotona = at home; going needs kotiin.
questions.explain: tulla + kotiin = to come home. Each verb needs its matching question: Missä? Mistä? Mihin?

questions.audio: Huomenna menen junalla Turkuun. Tulen takaisin sunnuntaina.
questions.q: How is the speaker travelling to Turku?
questions.explain: junalla = by train (adessive). Turkuun = to Turku (illative, strong grade).

questions.q: Build the question: “Are you coming from Tampere?”
questions.explain: Tampere takes outer cases, so from = -lta: Tampereelta.

questions.q: Build the sentence: “They are going to Helsinki by train.”
questions.explain: he menevät + Helsinkiin (illative, nk stays) + junalla (by train).
vasen has the stem vasemma-. To the left = allative: vasemma|lle.
On the right = adessive: oikea|lla. Where something is, so -lla.
suoraan = straight ahead. It is the illative form of suora (straight), used as a direction word.

questions.q: Which means *Turn left at the crossroads*?
wrong: vasemmalla = on the left; turning somewhere needs -lle.
questions.explain: Turning is movement, so the allative: vasemmalle = to the left.
questions.source: Uusi kielemme: Asking for and giving directions

questions.q: Read: *Apteekki on lähellä. Ensin menet suoraan. Sitten käännyt oikealle. Apteekki on vasemmalla.* Where is the pharmacy?
options: After a left turn, on the right
After a right turn, on the right
After a right turn, on the left
wrong: You turn oikealle (right); the pharmacy is vasemmalla (on the left).
questions.explain: käännyt oikealle = you turn right; vasemmalla = on the left.
questions.source: Uusi kielemme: Asking for and giving directions

questions.audio: Anteeksi, missä on kirjasto? – Menet suoraan. Sitten käännyt vasemmalle. Kirjasto on oikealla.
questions.q: Where is the library after the turn?
wrong: You turn left (vasemmalle); the library is on the right.
suoraan comes first, before the turn.
questions.explain: Kirjasto on oikealla = The library is on the right.
questions.source: Uusi kielemme: Asking for and giving directions

questions.audio: Bussipysäkki ei ole kaukana. Menet suoraan ja käännyt oikealle. Pysäkki on siellä.
wrong: ei ole kaukana = it is not far.
questions.explain: Bussipysäkki ei ole kaukana = The bus stop is not far (negation from World 1).
questions.source: Uusi kielemme: Asking for and giving directions

questions.q: Build the sentence: “Then you turn left.”
questions.explain: Sitten (then) + käännyt (you turn, nt → nn) + vasemmalle (to the left).

questions.q: Build the question: “Excuse me, where is the bus stop?”
questions.explain: Anteeksi first, then the question: missä on + the place.
questions.source: Uusi kielemme: Asking for and giving directions

questions.explain: Nähdään + a place in Missä? form. asema is an outer place: asema|lla.
A café is a building: inessive kahvila|ssa.
How you travel = adessive: taksi|lla.

questions.q: Read: *Hei Ali! Nähdään huomenna kello viisi torilla. Minä tulen bussilla. Terveisin, Leena* Where do they meet?
wrong: bussilla = by bus: how Leena travels.
questions.explain: torilla = at the market square (adessive).

questions.q: Which message tells your friend *I'm still at work*?
wrong: työ needs a case ending here.
questions.explain: olla + töissä = to be at work. Missä? → töissä.

questions.audio: Moi! Olen nyt junassa. Juna on vähän myöhässä. Olen asemalla kello kuusi.
questions.q: When will the speaker be at the station?
questions.explain: kello kuusi = at six o'clock. junassa = on the train (inside it).

questions.audio: Hei Tiina! Nähdään kahvilassa kauppakeskuksessa. Tulen sinne kello kolme.
options: At the shopping centre's bus stop
In a café in the shopping centre
questions.explain: kahvilassa kauppakeskuksessa = in a café in the shopping centre (two inessives).

questions.audio: Hei, tässä Juha. Olen vielä kotona. Bussi ei tule. Tulen autolla.
questions.q: Why is Juha still at home?
options: He is waiting for a taxi
wrong: He talks about the bus, not a train.
questions.explain: Bussi ei tule = The bus doesn't come, so he comes by car (autolla).

questions.q: Build the sentence: “See you at the station at six.”
questions.explain: Nähdään + place (asemalla) + time (kello kuusi). The place and time can swap.

questions.q: Build the sentence: “I'm already in the café.”
questions.explain: Olen + jo (already) + the place: kahvila|ssa.

writing.title: Where shall we meet?
writing.situation: Your friend Mari comes to your town by train on Saturday. Write her a message about where and when you meet.
writing.model:
Hei Mari!
Kiva, että tulet lauantaina! Nähdään rautatieasemalla kello kaksitoista. Minä tulen asemalle bussilla. Odotan sinua kahvilassa asemalla. Sitten menemme keskustaan. Siellä on hyvä ravintola. Illalla menemme kotiin.
Terveisin,
Sami
checklist: I wrote a greeting (Hei / Moi) and ended with my name
Where I meet uses a Missä? form (asemalla, kahvilassa)
Where I go uses a Mihin? form (keskustaan, kotiin)

writing.title: How to find my home
writing.situation: Your friend Ahmed visits you for the first time tomorrow. He comes by bus. Write him a message: how does he get from the bus to your home?
points: which bus he takes and where he gets off
something he sees on the way
writing.model:
Hei Ahmed!
Kiva, että tulet huomenna! Tulet bussilla 23. Jäät pois bussista torilla. Sitten menet suoraan. Risteyksessä käännyt vasemmalle. Apteekki on oikealla. Asun talossa numero 5. Se on vasemmalla. Odotan sinua kotona!
Terveisin,
Laura
checklist: I wrote a greeting and ended with my name
